question.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Area Bounded By a Curve When It Crosses the X-Axis Several Times
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/7ffd75051b71a3b8665ac68418ff24dac2124a6b7ff50633a0a5843df9cff196.png)

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y={x}^{5}-x$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
question.worked_solution:
First, we the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{4}-1) & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1)({x}^{2}+1) & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x(x-1)(x+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=\pm 1$ or $x=0.$ 
This gives us two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

For $x\in [-1,0]$, we have

$$
{A}_{1}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that for $x\in [0,1]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{2}=-{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}-({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}-({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$
